name: Boldo (Peumus boldus)
short: Case reports: jaundice and liver injury in 2 elderly people after boldo leaf tea; low tacrolimus in a transplant patient; raised INR on warfarin with boldo plus fenugreek. Rats: abortive, teratogenic.
text: Two case reports describe liver injury judged probably due to boldo after repeated drinking of boldo leaf infusions: an 87-year-old man and a 72-year-old woman each developed jaundice with raised liver enzymes and recovered after stopping; the authors say boldo may cause otherwise unexplained jaundice or abnormal liver enzymes, particularly in elderly people (and, in the second report, in elderly people with biliary tract disorders). In a rat study, a hydro-alcohol extract of dry boldo leaves and its alkaloid boldine showed abortive and teratogenic action and changed blood levels of bilirubin, cholesterol, glucose, the liver enzymes ALT and AST, and urea, although 90 days of administration caused no tissue changes; another rat study (20 male rats in four groups, 21 days) concluded that an aqueous boldo extract given by mouth had a neurotoxic effect at a clinical level, judged by the rotarod test; the abstract gives p=0.09 for the rotarod comparison of boldo alone with saline, and reports no difference between groups in the count of dopamine-producing neurons. A 2026 review says public health guidelines should emphasise avoiding self-medication with concentrated extracts and strict monitoring of patients with pre-existing liver conditions or who are pregnant. Two single case reports describe possible interactions: a kidney transplant recipient had subtherapeutic tacrolimus levels while taking boldo, which rose to target after boldo was stopped, and a woman taking warfarin had a raised INR while taking several natural products including boldo and fenugreek, which returned to normal when she stopped them and recurred when both were reintroduced; that interaction cannot be attributed to boldo alone.
